interactions.summary: The class moves from poetics into accusation: if Virgil had divine fire and used it for Augustus and empire, Jiang calls him the true betrayer, someone who weaponized sacred imagination instead of enlightening humanity.

claims.claim: Jiang identifies Virgil, not Lucifer, as the great betrayer because he received divine poetic power and redirected it toward imperial service.
Jiang argues that the inconsistencies in the Aeneid show what happens when divine fire is forced into a weapon of empire: some truth leaks out and resists the project.
For Jiang, divine poetry is meant to enlighten the world, not to be directed as a state weapon.
Jiang analogizes Virgil's betrayal to a hypothetical Jesus siding with Rome for personal gain instead of fulfilling his mission.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang imagines Augustus taking divine fire and turning it into an imperial weapon, with the poem's contradictions as sparks escaping the forge.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the divine fire does not want to be weaponized
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the sharpest statement of his anti-imperial reading of Virgil.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil becomes worse than a failed poet; he becomes a sacred traitor who sold revelation to empire.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It raises the moral stakes of the whole guide problem.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's description of what happens when sacred poetic power is conscripted into empire-building.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture escalates from Virgil knowing too much to Virgil actively betraying the divine source of poetry by serving imperial violence.
